articles.title: Global transportation impacts on wildlife mortality and emerging pathways for mitigation
articles.desc: Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine transportation are fundamental to modern human life, but vehicle collisions with wildlife inadvertently kill hundreds of millions of animals across 2000 vertebrate and invertebrate species annually; however, a comprehensive framework to assess and mitigate these mortalities is missing. We identified and compared the most up-to-date information regarding the impacts of transportation on wildlife mortality to determine cross-cutting solutions to this challenging problem. For example, numerous strategies, such as under- or overpasses traversing roads and railways that increase wildlife-habitat connectivity, policies that enforce reduced speed in areas with active wildlife, and passive sensors that detect wildlife to alert nearby ships and vehicles and enable mandatory speed reductions, can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions. We explored emerging technological advances that could help further reduce future wildlife-vehicle conflicts and provide a path forward for transportation systems. Specifically, we described how the combination of citizen science, artificial intelligence, targeted studies on wildlife demographic impacts, and cost-effective mitigation efforts will be powerful tools to inform needed future policies to decrease ship speed in areas with threatened whale species and reduce rates of wildlife mortality across ecosystems in a fast-moving world.

articles.title: Accounting for spatial dependence in random forests improves ecological understanding and enhances prediction
articles.desc: Random forests (RFs) are widely used in ecology to model complex, nonlinear relationships among environmental variables and to summarize fitted relationships through variable importance and interactions. However, many ecological datasets, particularly observational data collected across space, exhibit spatial dependence. If this spatial dependence is ignored, RFs can incorrectly attribute importance to predictors that serve at least partly as proxies for spatial location. In this study, we evaluate how accounting for spatial dependence changes both predictive performance and ecological interpretation. Using simulations with known data-generating mechanisms and an analysis of 1061 North American river catchments, we compare standard RFs, RFs with spatial residual modeling, and a model-agnostic spatial decorrelation transformation. The simulations show that spatially structured noise variables and raw coordinates can receive inflated importance in standard RF workflows, whereas decorrelation reduces these artifacts and recovers the relevant predictors more consistently. In the river flow application, decorrelation improves held-out prediction and shifts interpretation from broad spatially smooth gradients toward hydrologic and soil variables with more direct mechanistic links to flow seasonality.

articles.title: Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, stratigraphic integrity, and confirming early inland dispersal: Evaluating peopling of the Americas modeling
articles.desc: Statistical models shape debates over the timing and geography of the initial peopling of the Americas, but their value depends on testing their assumptions against archaeological evidence. We examine the Apparent Stratigraphic Integrity Index (ASI), used to infer postdepositional mixing at Late Pleistocene sites and support a relatively late occupation of temperate North America. ASI describes vertical discontinuity in binned artifact-frequency profiles; it does not directly measure artifact movement or stratigraphic integrity. At Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, Idaho, the 5-centimeter absolute-elevation bins used to calculate ASI do not reflect the actual stratigraphic positions of artifacts across the irregular LU2 surface on which LU3 loess accumulated. The resulting ASI value cannot support claims of large-scale vertical mixing. Independent chronological, stratigraphic, pedogenic, archaeological, and excavation evidence supports the integrity of the ∼16,000–calibrated-years-before-the-present occupation. Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe provides early inland evidence expected under coastal-migration models, showing that models should be evaluated against archaeological evidence rather than used to override it.

articles.title: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.desc: Carbon removal markets lack a standardized, quantitative measure of permanence risk. Inspired by value at risk in financial markets, we propose carbon at risk (CaR): a probabilistic measure of the shortfall between contracted removals and realized storage at a given confidence level and time horizon. We calibrate CaR in two proof-of-concept applications: forest carbon, where Monte Carlo simulations driven by satellite fire data yield a single-project 95% CaR of more than 70% over 200 years for California, and geological storage, where simulations using the Storage Security Calculator show that the 95% CaR ranges from 0.15% (well-regulated offshore) to 17% (poorly regulated onshore). Combining technologies in a portfolio can help manage tail risk cost-effectively. The minimum cost of meeting a permanence target depends on the magnitude and correlation structure of key risk factors. CaR provides a technology-agnostic basis for risk-calibrated buffer sizing, insurance pricing and reserve-fund design, over both policy- and climate-relevant horizons.

articles.desc: Forest ecosystems are shaped by the consequences of management activities, as well as through an increase in tree damage and mortality caused by climate change. articles.title: A risk framework for addressing nature’s harmful contributions to people
articles.desc: Some aspects of nature can be harmful to people and have become contentious issues in biodiversity research and policy. This Perspective proposes a new conceptual framework for assessing and managing nature’s harmful contributions to people, drawing parallels with the concept of climate risk.

articles.title: OECMs contribute to strengthening existing networks of conservation areas
articles.desc: Our analysis provides a global assessment of the structural configuration of conservation networks that comprise both protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), offering new insight into how OECMs are strengthening current protected area networks.

articles.title: Non-ribosomal peptide diversity is driven by multiple evolutionary processes
articles.desc: Non-ribosomal peptides are microbial secondary metabolites that are synthesized by very large modular synthetase enzymes. Using a recombination-aware phylogenetic framework, we find that the evolution of these synthetases is driven by recombination and is subject to complex evolutionary forces.

articles.title: A mid-Cretaceous island as a cradle of Southeast Asian plant biodiversity
articles.desc: Here the authors present an assemblage of plant fossils three-dimensionally preserved in amber, including 392 angiosperm morphospecies and 152 non-angiosperm morphospecies represented by flowers, fruit, leaves and other plant parts. This assemblage documents exceptionally diverse flora in the mid-Cretaceous.

articles.title: Temporal links in avian migration schedules across the annual cycle
articles.desc: Analysing the complete annual life cycle from tracking data among 83 species of migratory landbirds across six continents, the authors identify strong temporal links in schedules of migratory periods but a temporal reset during the extended non-breeding period.

articles.title: Maternal inheritance accelerates sex chromosome degeneration and mitonuclear coevolution in a brood parasitic bird
articles.desc: Comparative genomics across eight songbird species links strong ecological selection on maternally inherited egg colour phenotypes to both accelerated W chromosome degeneration and mitonuclear coevolution in the brood parasitic cuckoo finch (Anomalospiza imberbis), reflecting the consequences of genetic hitchhiking for non-recombining components of the genome.

articles.title: Other effective area-based conservation measures may enhance global conservation networks
articles.desc: A typology of the ways in which other effective area-based conservation measures can structurally contribute to protected-area networks identifies opportunities for optimization and consolidation of conservation areas.

articles.title: A fully marine stem amphibian from the Late Triassic of China
articles.desc: A new fossil species of a Late Triassic stem amphibian lacks the permeable skin of present-day amphibians, and its find location, taphonomic context and geochemistry suggest that it maintained a fully marine lifestyle.

articles.title: C4 photosynthetic pathway fluxes in transgenic rice plants
articles.desc: Crop plants such as rice employ the C3 photosynthesis pathway; however, the C4 pathway has a generally greater yield and water use efficiency. Rice transgenic for several C4 enzymes shows metabolic fluxes corresponding to four core C4 reactions.

articles.title: Regulation of the 22-nt antiviral silencing pathway in tomato by two RNA viruses
articles.desc: The DCL2b-mediated 22-nt sRNA pathway is critical for tomato antiviral defence. Viral infection induces DCL2b transcription and promotes its cytoplasmic accumulation, enhancing antiviral activity while limiting nuclear miR6026 feedback.

articles.title: Regional climate change approaches Paris limits
articles.desc: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02797-5 It has been surprisingly difficult to calculate how much warming different regions of the Earth have experienced since pre-industrial times. Now, research shows that in most land regions, the temperature thresholds that governments agreed to in Paris to keep below are already dangerously close.

articles.title: All IPCC AR6 regions are close to their 1.5 °C- and 2 °C-equivalent warming limits
articles.desc: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02790-y Climate targets are set for global temperatures, but what they mean regionally is less clear. Here the authors quantify the amount of human-induced warming in individual IPCC regions and find that, by 2025, they had reached 90–94% (65–76%) of their expected warming levels at the 1.5 °C (2 °C) global warming thresholds.
